reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / GOLD & ATS guidelines
clinicalPearls: Silicosis is a fibrotic lung disease caused by inhaling crystalline silica dust, seen in mining, quarrying, sandblasting, stone-cutting, and engineered-stone work
Chronic silicosis develops after prolonged exposure and may be asymptomatic initially, later causing exertional dyspnoea and cough
Accelerated and acute (silicoproteinosis) forms follow intense exposure and progress far more rapidly
Chest imaging classically shows small upper-zone nodular opacities, sometimes with eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes
Simple nodular disease can coalesce into progressive massive fibrosis, producing large conglomerate masses and significant impairment
Silica exposure substantially increases susceptibility to tuberculosis (silicotuberculosis), which should be actively sought and treated
There is no treatment that reverses fibrosis; management focuses on stopping exposure, supportive care, and screening for and treating complications
Silica is also associated with increased risks of lung cancer, chronic airflow obstruction, and certain autoimmune diseases
reference.pathophysiology: Inhaled crystalline silica particles reaching the alveoli are taken up by macrophages. The reactive silica surface is toxic to these macrophages, triggering activation of inflammasome pathways, cell death, and release of inflammatory cytokines and reactive oxygen species. This provokes recruitment of further inflammatory cells and stimulation of fibroblasts, which lay down collagen to form the characteristic silicotic nodules. Continued or intense exposure sustains the cycle, with nodules enlarging and coalescing into progressive massive fibrosis, while impaired macrophage function increases vulnerability to mycobacterial infection.
additionalDifferentials: Other pneumoconioses such as coal workers' pneumoconiosis
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and other interstitial lung diseases
Metastatic or miliary nodular lung disease
additionalInvestigations: Chest radiography with attention to upper-zone nodularity and eggshell nodal calcification
High-resolution CT to characterise nodules and detect progressive massive fibrosis
Pulmonary function testing to quantify restrictive, obstructive, or mixed impairment
Screening for tuberculosis given the heightened risk
Detailed occupational exposure history including engineered-stone and sandblasting work
redFlags: New constitutional symptoms, haemoptysis, or cavitation suggesting tuberculosis or malignancy
Rapidly progressive breathlessness indicating accelerated or acute silicosis
Enlarging conglomerate masses consistent with progressive massive fibrosis
Development of respiratory failure or cor pulmonale
reference.prognosis: Chronic simple silicosis may remain stable with limited impairment, but progressive massive fibrosis, accelerated, and acute forms carry a poor prognosis with progressive respiratory failure; the lifelong increased risk of tuberculosis and lung cancer means continued surveillance is important, and outcomes improve when exposure ceases early.
pitfalls: Failing to elicit an occupational silica exposure history, especially newer engineered-stone work
Overlooking coexisting tuberculosis in a patient with silicosis
Attributing all nodular change to silicosis without considering malignancy
Not removing the worker from ongoing dust exposure
management: Immediate and permanent removal from crystalline silica exposure with dust control and respiratory protection, as there is no therapy that reverses the fibrosis
Smoking cessation and vaccination against influenza and pneumococcus to limit respiratory decline and infection
Active screening for and treatment of tuberculosis, including latent infection, given the heightened silicotuberculosis risk
Supportive respiratory care with bronchodilators, pulmonary rehabilitation and supplemental oxygen for hypoxaemia
Serial chest imaging and lung function testing to monitor for progressive massive fibrosis and lung cancer
Referral for lung transplantation assessment in advanced or progressive fibrosis with respiratory failure
Occupational health notification, compensation advice and workplace exposure reduction
